specPoints.text: describe the effects of changes in surface area of a solid, concentration of a solution, pressure of a gas, temperature and the use of a catalyst on the rate of a reaction
describe experiments to investigate the effects of changes in surface area of a solid, concentration of a solution, temperature and the use of a catalyst on the rate of a reaction

primer.text: From Energetics you already know how to follow a reaction with a thermometer. This note follows it with a stopwatch instead, describing the experiments that test how surface area, concentration, temperature and catalysts change the pace of a reaction. It closes by reading the same story off rate graphs.

lessons.title: Experiments on surface area and concentration
sourceHeadings: Effect of surface area of a solid on the rate of reaction
Effect of concentration of a solution on the rate of reaction
lessons.opening: Two experiments anchor the surface area and concentration stories: marble chips fizzing in acid, and a cloudy cross disappearing under thiosulfate. This lesson walks both methods and the measurements each one collects.
keyPoints: The surface area experiment adds marble chips to dilute hydrochloric acid and collects the gas produced.
A delivery tube feeds the gas into an inverted measuring cylinder in a water trough.
Gas volume over a fixed time is measured, then the run repeats with different chip sizes.
The concentration experiment watches a cross under the flask disappear as the mixture clouds.
Sodium thiosulfate is diluted with water to give different concentrations for each repeat.

low.restatement: Bigger chips or stronger acid should change how fast gas bubbles appear or how quickly a cross vanishes under cloudy liquid. Each experiment changes one factor, times the result and repeats with a new size or strength.
low.analogy: It is like timing how fast sugar vanishes in stirred tea: one lump versus crushed sugar, or weak tea versus strong.
low.examPointer: Name the measured quantity, gas volume or disappearance time, and the factor varied in each method.

medium.restatement: For surface area, marble chips react with dilute hydrochloric acid and the gas collected in a fixed time is compared across chip sizes. For concentration, sodium thiosulfate of different strengths reacts with acid while a stopwatch times how long a marked cross stays visible through the clouding mixture.
medium.analogy: The first is a race of bubbling, the second a race of fading; both stop the clock the moment a fixed landmark is reached.
medium.examPointer: Describe apparatus and timing for both methods, and state how the factor is varied between repeats.

check.stem: What is measured in the marble chip experiment?

options.text: The volume of gas produced in a fixed time
options.explanation: Gas volume over a set time tracks how fast the chips react with the acid.

options.text: The temperature rise of the acid
options.explanation: No thermometer reading is the measured quantity in this rate experiment.

options.text: The mass of chips dissolved after an hour
options.explanation: The method measures gas, and the window is a fixed short time.

options.text: The colour change of the solution
options.explanation: Colour watching belongs to the thiosulfate experiment.

check.stem: Why is the measuring cylinder inverted in a water trough?

options.text: To collect and measure the volume of gas given off
options.explanation: Gas bubbles into the inverted cylinder and displaces water, so the reading gives the volume.

options.text: To keep the acid warm during the reaction
options.explanation: The trough holds water for collection, not temperature control.

options.text: To dilute the acid as it reacts
options.explanation: The acid never enters the trough.

options.text: To stop the chips from floating
options.explanation: The chips stay in the conical flask throughout.

check.stem: How are different concentrations of sodium thiosulfate prepared?

options.text: By mixing different volumes of thiosulfate solution with water to dilute it
options.explanation: Diluting with water gives a set of strengths to compare against the acid.

options.text: By heating the thiosulfate to different temperatures
options.explanation: Heating varies temperature, not concentration.

options.text: By using different acids each time
options.explanation: The acid stays the same; the thiosulfate varies.

options.text: By adding more marble chips
options.explanation: Marble chips belong to the surface area experiment.

check.stem: When does the stopwatch stop in the concentration experiment?

options.text: When the cross under the flask can no longer be seen from above
options.explanation: The vanishing cross is the fixed landmark that marks the same extent of clouding each run.

options.text: When the first bubbles appear
options.explanation: No bubbling landmark is used in this experiment.

options.text: After a countdown of thirty seconds
options.explanation: The endpoint is observed, not a preset time.

options.text: When the mixture turns colourless again
options.explanation: The mixture clouds and stays cloudy within the timing window.

check.stem: Increasing the concentration of the thiosulfate has what effect on the result?

options.text: The rate increases because more particles occupy the same volume
options.explanation: A denser particle crowd collides more often, so the cross vanishes sooner.

options.text: The rate decreases because the solution is thinner
options.explanation: Dilution lowers rate; increasing concentration raises it.

options.text: The rate is unchanged because acid amount is fixed
options.explanation: The factor tested does change the rate even with fixed acid.

options.text: The rate falls to zero at high concentration
options.explanation: Nothing stops the reaction at high concentration.

check.stem: State where the gas is collected in the surface area experiment.
check.modelAnswer: A delivery tube feeds the gas into an inverted measuring cylinder standing in a water trough.

check.stem: State what is watched in the concentration experiment as the mixture clouds.
check.modelAnswer: A cross drawn under the flask is watched until it disappears as the mixture clouds.

check.stem: Explain why sodium thiosulfate is diluted with water in the concentration experiment.
check.modelAnswer: Diluting the sodium thiosulfate with water gives reaction mixtures of different concentrations, so the effect of concentration on the rate can be tested.

check.stem: Two chip sizes are tested and the gas volume read after the same fixed time. State the comparison this timing choice allows.
check.modelAnswer: Reading every gas volume over the same fixed time means the two chip sizes can be compared fairly, since only the surface area differs between the runs.

lessons.title: Experiments on temperature and catalysts
sourceHeadings: Effect of temperature on the rate of reaction
Effect of a catalyst on the rate of reaction
lessons.opening: Two more experiments complete the set: magnesium in warmed acid, and hydrogen peroxide breaking down with and without a black powder. This lesson times both and explains what each comparison proves.
keyPoints: The temperature experiment heats dilute hydrochloric acid to a set temperature in a water bath.
A strip of magnesium is added, the stopwatch started, and the time taken for the metal to dissolve is recorded.
The experiment is repeated at different temperatures and the results compared.
The catalyst experiment adds manganese(IV) oxide to hydrogen peroxide and collects the oxygen produced.
The run is repeated without the catalyst so the two gas volumes can be compared.

low.restatement: Warm the acid to a chosen temperature, drop in magnesium and time how long it takes to vanish; then try a hotter bath. For catalysts, run the peroxide reaction with the powder and again without, and compare the gas collected.
low.analogy: One test is timing how fast sugar dissolves in warm versus cool tea; the other is checking whether a pinch of powder makes a bottle fizz faster.
low.examPointer: State the timed quantity and the comparison run for each experiment, with the factor varied named.

medium.restatement: Dilute hydrochloric acid is warmed to a set temperature in a water bath, magnesium is added, and the time for the metal to fully dissolve is recorded before repeating at other temperatures. In the catalyst experiment the oxygen collected from hydrogen peroxide in a fixed time is compared with and without manganese(IV) oxide.
medium.analogy: The magnesium race gets faster as the water bath climbs, while the peroxide test is a race run twice, once with a helper and once without.
medium.examPointer: Quote the water bath, the dissolve time and the with-and-without comparison when describing these methods.

check.stem: What times the end of the temperature experiment?

options.text: The moment the magnesium strip has fully dissolved
options.explanation: The dissolving of the metal is the fixed landmark for the stopwatch.

options.text: The moment the acid starts bubbling
options.explanation: Bubbling begins almost at once, so it marks nothing useful.

options.text: A fixed countdown of one minute
options.explanation: The time is measured, not preset.

options.text: When the water bath reaches temperature
options.explanation: That happens before the reaction even starts.

check.stem: Why does the acid sit in a water bath before the magnesium is added?

options.text: To bring the acid to a set temperature before the reaction is timed
options.explanation: The bath fixes the starting temperature so each run tests a known value.

options.text: To dilute the acid to a working concentration
options.explanation: Dilution is not the bath's job; water outside the flask never mixes in.

options.text: To keep the magnesium from reacting too slowly
options.explanation: The bath sets the temperature; it does not act on the metal directly.

options.text: To prevent the acid from evaporating
options.explanation: Evaporation is not the concern in this short experiment.

check.stem: In the catalyst experiment, what is collected in the inverted measuring cylinder?

options.text: The oxygen produced by the breakdown of hydrogen peroxide
options.explanation: Hydrogen peroxide decomposes to oxygen and water, and the gas is collected.

options.text: Hydrogen given off by the catalyst
options.explanation: The catalyst does not supply hydrogen; peroxide decomposition makes oxygen.

options.text: Steam from the warm solution
options.explanation: The experiment runs at room temperature.

options.text: Air drawn in as the liquid contracts
options.explanation: Gas flows out of the flask, not air into it.

check.stem: Why run the peroxide experiment a second time without the catalyst?

options.text: To provide a comparison that shows the catalyst's effect on the rate
options.explanation: Without the with-and-without pair, the gas volumes would prove nothing.

options.text: To use up the leftover peroxide safely
options.explanation: Safety disposal is not the experimental reason.

options.text: To double the amount of oxygen collected
options.explanation: The runs are separate measurements, not pooled samples.

options.text: To prove the catalyst is used up
options.explanation: Catalysts are not consumed, and this comparison does not test that.

check.stem: Which factor is deliberately changed between the two peroxide runs?

options.text: The presence of the manganese(IV) oxide catalyst
options.explanation: The catalyst is the only factor the pair of runs varies.

options.text: The concentration of the peroxide
options.explanation: The peroxide stays the same so the comparison is fair.

options.text: The volume of the measuring cylinder
options.explanation: Apparatus stays fixed across the runs.

options.text: The time allowed for collection
options.explanation: The fixed time is what makes the two volumes comparable.

check.stem: State what is measured in the temperature experiment once the magnesium strip is added.
check.modelAnswer: A stopwatch is started and the time taken for the magnesium metal to dissolve is recorded.

check.stem: State the catalyst added to hydrogen peroxide in the catalyst experiment.
check.modelAnswer: Manganese(IV) oxide is added to hydrogen peroxide, and the oxygen produced is collected.

check.stem: Explain why the catalyst experiment is repeated without the catalyst.
check.modelAnswer: Repeating the run without the catalyst gives a control gas volume, so the two runs can be compared to show how much faster the catalysed decomposition is.

check.stem: A student heats the acid to 40 degrees Celsius for one run and 60 degrees Celsius for another. State which piece of apparatus keeps each run at its set temperature.
check.modelAnswer: A water bath holds each run at its set temperature while the dilute hydrochloric acid is heated.

lessons.title: Factors, graphs and the economic angle
sourceHeadings: The effect of increased concentration or pressure
lessons.opening: Four factors govern how fast reactions run, and each leaves a fingerprint on the rate graph. This lesson collects the fingerprints and adds the industrial reason anyone cares.
keyPoints: The factors affecting rate are concentration or pressure, temperature, surface area of solids and catalysts.
A faster reaction shows a steeper starting gradient that becomes horizontal sooner.
Graphs for changed conditions still finish at the same amount of product.
Increasing the concentration, pressure, temperature or surface area each increases the rate of reaction.
Industry favours higher rates because faster production is more efficient and sustainable.

low.restatement: Every factor that packs particles closer or makes them livelier steepens the start of the graph. The curve flattens at the same final product amount, and industry chases that steep start for cheaper production.
low.analogy: It is like three routes up the same hill: steeper starts reach the top sooner, but the summit height never changes.
low.examPointer: Sketch or describe the steeper-start-same-plateau shape and name the four rate factors.

medium.restatement: Compared with the slower condition, a faster reaction line starts with a steeper gradient and flattens sooner while forming the same amount of product. Concentration, pressure, temperature, surface area and catalysts are the levers, and raising the first four raises the rate that industry prizes.
medium.analogy: Two commuters reach the same office, but the express train gets there earlier and waits; the destination is fixed, only the pace differs.
medium.examPointer: Compare two lines by gradient, plateau timing and final product, and tie faster rates to production efficiency.

check.stem: What shape distinguishes the graph of a faster reaction from a slower one?

options.text: A steeper starting gradient that becomes horizontal sooner
options.explanation: Faster reactions climb quickly and plateau early.

options.text: A shallower gradient that plateaus later
options.explanation: That describes the slower reaction.

options.text: A curve that never levels off
options.explanation: Reactions end when reactants run out, so all curves flatten.

options.text: A line that dips before rising
options.explanation: Product amount never falls in these graphs.

check.stem: Two reactions differ only in temperature. What is true of their final product amounts?

options.text: They form the same amount of product
options.explanation: Temperature changes the pace, not the final yield fixed by the starting amounts.

options.text: The hotter one makes more product
options.explanation: The plateau is set by the reactants, not the speed.

options.text: The cooler one makes more product
options.explanation: Neither temperature wins on amount.

options.text: Neither reaction makes any product
options.explanation: Both proceed, just at different paces.

check.stem: Which list names all four factors that can affect the rate of a reaction?

options.text: Concentration or pressure, temperature, surface area, catalyst
options.explanation: Those four are the levers named in the factor list.

options.text: Colour, temperature, surface area, catalyst
options.explanation: Colour does not change the rate.

options.text: Concentration, volume of container, light, catalyst
options.explanation: Light is not on this list, and container volume alone is not the factor.

options.text: Pressure, temperature, mass of products, catalyst
options.explanation: Product mass is an outcome, not a rate factor.

check.stem: Why are faster rates of industrial interest?

options.text: A higher rate implies a higher rate of production and a more efficient, sustainable process
options.explanation: Faster chemistry makes more product per hour, cutting cost and waste.

options.text: Faster reactions always cost nothing to run
options.explanation: Speed has costs, such as heating or catalysts; the benefit is throughput.

options.text: Faster reactions avoid the need for reactants
options.explanation: Reactants are still consumed however fast the reaction runs.

options.text: Faster reactions are always safer
options.explanation: Safety depends on the process, not the pace alone.

check.stem: Powdering a solid reactant instead of using one lump does what to the rate graph?

options.text: It steepens the start because more surface is exposed to the other reactant
options.explanation: Powder exposes more particles at once, so the early line climbs faster.

options.text: It lowers the final plateau
options.explanation: The same amount of product forms either way.

options.text: It has no effect because mass is unchanged
options.explanation: Mass is unchanged but the exposed area is not.

options.text: It makes the reaction endothermic
options.explanation: Energy direction is unrelated to surface area.

check.stem: State the four factors affecting the rate of a reaction.
check.modelAnswer: The factors are concentration or pressure, temperature, the surface area of solids, and catalysts.

check.stem: State how a faster reaction looks different on a rate graph.
check.modelAnswer: A faster reaction shows a steeper starting gradient that becomes horizontal sooner.

check.stem: Explain why graphs for reactions run under changed conditions all finish at the same amount of product.
check.modelAnswer: Changing the conditions only alters how quickly the reaction reaches completion, not how much product the limiting amounts of reactants can make, so every curve levels at the same final amount.

check.stem: A chemical plant wants to make its product faster without hiring more staff. State the commercial benefit of raising the rate of reaction.
check.modelAnswer: Faster production is more efficient and sustainable, cutting the time and energy cost per batch for the plant.

glossary.definition: How quickly reactants are used up or products are formed in a chemical reaction.
The amount of dissolved reactant in a given volume of solution.
A tube that carries gas from the reaction flask to the collecting measuring cylinder.
A substance that speeds up a reaction without being consumed, such as manganese(IV) oxide for peroxide.
The steepness of a rate graph line; steeper means more product per unit time.

workedExample.prompt: a) A 2 cm3 cube is cut up into 8 smaller cubes. Show that this doubles its total surface area. b) State the four factors that affect the rate of a reaction and the direction of each effect. c) On a graph of product amount against time, how does a faster reaction differ from a slower one?
steps: a) One 2 cm3 cube has a surface area of 24 cm2; the same cube cut into 8 cubes has a surface area of 48 cm2 — 48 / 24 = 2, so the total surface area doubles (surface area increases as particle size decreases).

b) Increasing the concentration of a solution (or pressure of a gas), increasing the temperature, and increasing the surface area of a solid each increase the rate; adding a catalyst also increases the rate.
c) The faster reaction has a steeper starting gradient and becomes horizontal sooner, but both lines finish at the same final amount of product.
workedExample.finalAnswer: a) 24 cm2 → 48 cm2, a doubling. b) Concentration/pressure, temperature, surface area, catalyst — all increase the rate. c) Steeper start, same plateau.
